fixes.explanation: That's it, friend. Micah says, "there is no cluster to eat, no early fig that I crave." He compares himself to someone gleaning a vineyard, and that gleaner comes up with no cluster. It's like reaching into the cookie box at the end of the party and feeling nothing but crumbs.

I see why the fig grabbed you, because it's right there in the verse. But Micah says there is "…no early fig that I crave." So it's not even one. That's like digging in the cookie tin for the last cookie, and the tin is bare.

Oh, that would be a great day to be a gleaner! Arms full, big smile, maybe a little dance. Micah says the opposite, though: "there is no cluster to eat…" The prophet Micah says he's like a gleaner with no cluster and no early fig.

Yes. Micah says, "They all lie in wait for blood; they hunt one another with a net." A net is what you'd think of for hunting animals, and here the people hunt one another. I'll say it plainly: this part is heavy.

Yep. Micah says, "the prince and the judge demand a bribe." A judge is the one who's supposed to be fair, and this one has his hand out. That's a referee checking his pocket before he blows the whistle. I think that's a heavy thing to see in the leaders.
Sacrifice is a religious word, so I get the pull. But Micah never says the prince and the judge demand one. He says they "…demand a bribe." That's the picture here, nothing about the altar.

That's right. Micah says, "When the powerful utters his evil desire, they all conspire together." One powerful person speaks his evil desire, and then they all conspire together. That's exactly what the verse says.

Actually, that one is word for word what Micah says. "When the powerful utters his evil desire, they all conspire together." The powerful person speaks, and then they all conspire together. It's right there in verse 3.

Yes. Micah says, "Seal the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms." Right before that, he says not to rely on a friend or trust in a companion. Then he points to someone in your arms. It's a heavy line.

Micah has been talking about the people around him, so the city makes sense. But in this verse he says, "A man’s enemies are the members of his own household." The word he uses is household, not city. Just before it, he names a son, a daughter and a daughter-in-law.

That sounds like a reasonable plan, but it's not what Micah says. Just before this he says, "Do not rely on a friend; do not trust in a companion." What he says he will do is this: "But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation."
